scenes.heading: Design an Uber Data Platform
scenes.narration: Let us design a platform for a ride-hailing marketplace, handling high-volume geospatial trip events, real-time pricing, and analytics across a two-sided marketplace.

scenes.heading: Core requirements
bullets: Ingest driver and rider location streams
Real-time supply, demand, and surge pricing
Historical analytics for pricing and ops
scenes.narration: The platform must ingest continuous location pings from drivers and riders at massive scale. It needs real-time views of supply and demand per region to drive surge pricing decisions. It must record trips and payments with exactly-once semantics, because double-charging or lost trips are unacceptable. And it must retain rich history so data scientists can model pricing, ETAs, and marketplace health.

scenes.heading: Streaming-first architecture
steps: Location events into Kafka by region
CDC feeds the lake for analytics
scenes.narration: Location and trip events flow into Kafka, partitioned by geographic region so each area's stream can be processed independently. Stream-processing jobs compute rolling supply and demand aggregates per region. The surge pricing engine reads those live aggregates to set multipliers within seconds. Completed trips and payments are written transactionally to an operational datastore for correctness. Change data capture then streams those committed records into the lake, feeding batch analytics and modeling.

scenes.heading: Operational store vs analytical lake
scenes.narration: The operational store handles low-latency, exactly-once writes and point reads that the live app depends on, such as fetching an active trip. The analytical lake is built for high-throughput scans and huge aggregations that power data science, pricing models, and dashboards. Keeping them separate but linked by change data capture lets each be optimized for its job, so heavy analytics never slow down the app serving riders and drivers.

scenes.heading: Handling geospatial data
bullets: Index locations with a geohash or H3 grid
Aggregate supply and demand per cell
Cells become the unit of surge pricing
scenes.narration: Geospatial handling is central to a ride platform. Raw latitude and longitude are hard to aggregate, so locations are indexed into a spatial grid using a scheme like geohash or Uber's own H3 hexagons. Supply and demand are then aggregated per grid cell, which makes nearest-driver lookups and regional counts fast. Those cells become the natural unit for surge pricing, letting the platform raise prices precisely where demand outstrips supply without affecting neighboring areas.

scenes.heading: Guaranteeing correctness
bullets: Idempotent writes keyed by trip id
Exactly-once processing in the stream layer
scenes.narration: Because money and trust are on the line, correctness is enforced at several levels. Writes are made idempotent by keying them on the trip id, so a retried request cannot create a duplicate trip. The streaming layer uses exactly-once processing so events are neither lost nor double-counted. Payments are written transactionally so a charge and its record commit together. And periodic reconciliation jobs compare operational and analytical records to catch and flag any discrepancies before they reach customers.

scenes.text: Partition by geography, compute demand in-stream, keep trips transactional, and bridge to the lake with CDC for analytics.
scenes.narration: Partition streams by geography for locality, compute supply and demand in-stream for real-time pricing, keep trips and payments strictly transactional for correctness, and bridge to an analytical lake with change data capture so operations and analytics each run on the right engine.
